summary: Registers the image/tiff-fx MIME sub-type for the TIFF-FX encoding used by Internet fax. It was replaced by RFC 3950.

plainLanguage.summary: A fax image file gets an official name tag so email programs know what it is. It has been replaced by RFC 3950.

subtitle: Official registration of a MIME type for fax images in TIFF-FX format.

tldr.problem: The TIFF-FX file format for Internet fax needed an official MIME type so email systems could recognize and handle the files correctly.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC registers the MIME media type image/tiff-fx with the IANA, formally associating it with TIFF-FX fax image data.
tldr.outcome: Email clients and fax systems now have a standard way to label TIFF-FX fax files. This specification was replaced by RFC 3950.

sections.title: What is TIFF-FX
sections.content:
TIFF-FX (Tag Image File Format Fax eXtended) is a file format for sending faxes over the Internet. It is defined in RFC 2301, which specifies a TIFF-based structure compatible with the existing ITU-T fax standards for Group 3 black-and-white, grayscale and color facsimile.

TIFF has long been used for storing fax images in applications like store-and-forward messaging systems. TIFF-FX provides a standardized structure optimized for Internet fax transmission and designed for devices with low memory or systems that need to process pages one at a time without loading the entire file.
sections.plainLanguage: TIFF-FX is a way to store fax images as computer files. It is based on TIFF, which is already used for pictures, but tweaked specifically to work well with fax machines and the Internet.

sections.title: Features and Capabilities
sections.content:
TIFF-FX can describe many kinds of image data: bilevel (black and white only), grayscale, palette-color, full-color and mixed content images. It includes several compression schemes allowing developers to choose the best trade-off between file size and processing time for their use.

TIFF-FX is designed to be extensible and to evolve gracefully as new needs arise. The format is flexible enough to support existing ITU-T fax recommendations while remaining open to future extensions.
sections.plainLanguage: TIFF-FX can store black-and-white faxes, color faxes, or a mix. It has several ways to compress the image to make files smaller, and you can add new features to it later without breaking old programs.

sections.title: MIME Type Registration
sections.content:
This RFC formally registers the MIME media type image/tiff-fx with the IANA. The type refers to TIFF-FX Profiles J, C, L and M encoded image data and any future TIFF-FX extensions, or subsets thereof. The content type may also be used for black-and-white image data encoded using TIFF-FX Profiles S or F.

No required parameters are specified for this MIME type, and no optional parameters are defined. The encoding is binary data, and base64 encoding should be used on transport mechanisms that cannot handle binary data directly. The file extension for TIFF-FX files is .TFX, and the Macintosh file type code is TFX.

The magic numbers for identifying TIFF-FX files are the same as standard TIFF: 49 49 2A 00 hex for little-endian byte order, and 4D 4D 00 2A hex for big-endian byte order. Applications using this media type include imaging, fax, messaging and multimedia systems.
sections.plainLanguage: The official name for TIFF-FX in email is image/tiff-fx. When a computer sees that label on a file, it knows the file is a fax image. The file also has a special pattern at the beginning so programs can recognize it even without the email label.

sections.title: Security and Status
sections.content:
TIFF-FX uses a structure that stores image data and attributes describing that image. The fields currently defined in the TIFF-FX specification are descriptive in nature and provide information useful for viewing and rendering images. These fields do not induce particular behavior by the recipient application, so they do not create additional security risks beyond those of handling any image file.

Because TIFF-FX has an extensible structure, it would theoretically be possible for fields to be defined in the future that could induce particular actions, but such processing instructions are inconsistent with the goals of the TIFF-FX specification and are not supported.

RFC 3250 was obsoleted by RFC 3950, which revised the MIME type registration.
sections.plainLanguage: TIFF-FX files are just image data and labels. They do not contain instructions that could make your computer do something unexpected. The newer RFC 3950 replaced this one.
